pages.text: Aratus of Sicyon was a political leader and military commander in ancient Greece. When he was a young boy, his father was killed in a coup. Aratus had to escape from his home city to stay safe.

Aratus grew up in the city of Argos. When he was an adult, he wanted to free his home city of Sicyon from tyranny. In 251 BC, he led an expedition of exiles and successfully freed Sicyon without fighting a big war. He then welcomed back the other exiled citizens.

After freeing Sicyon, Aratus helped his city join the Achaean League. This was a group of Greek cities working together. Aratus was elected as the leader, called strategos, many times. Under his guidance, the League grew larger and welcomed many new cities.

Aratus led many military campaigns to expand the League. One of his most famous actions was taking over the strong fortress of Acrocorinth. Later, when Sparta became a threat under King Cleomenes III, Aratus asked the king of Macedon for help.

With help from Macedon, the Achaean forces defeated Sparta at the Battle of Sellasia. Later, Aratus advised the new king of Macedon during the Social War. Aratus died in 213 BC, and historical reports state he was poisoned by the king.

B1-B2.headline: The Life and Leadership of Aratus

pages.text: Aratus of Sicyon was a prominent Hellenistic politician and military commander born in 271 BC. Following the murder of his father during a political coup, seven-year-old Aratus was smuggled out of Sicyon by his aunt. He spent his youth in exile in Argos.

In 251 BC, Aratus led a group of fellow exiles to liberate Sicyon from tyranny using scaling ladders at night. Upon taking power, he recalled hundreds of banished citizens and decided to attach Sicyon to the Achaean League, marking the first time a non-Achaean polis joined.

Elected as strategos of the Achaean League in 245 BC, Aratus held the position seventeen times. His leadership was marked by territorial expansion, including the capture of the Macedonian-held citadel of Acrocorinth, which had previously been considered impregnable.

When Spartan King Cleomenes III conquered several Achaean cities and won victories against the League, Aratus negotiated a crucial alliance with Antigonus III Doson of Macedon. The joint Achaean and Macedonian forces ultimately defeated Cleomenes at the Battle of Sellasia.

During the subsequent Social War against the Aetolian League, Aratus served as a primary advisor to the Macedonian king Philip V. Aratus died in 213 BC, with ancient accounts alleging that he was poisoned by Philip after a political dispute.

Aratus of Sicyon was a pivotal Hellenistic statesman and military commander whose career shaped the political landscape of Greece. His early life was disrupted by a coup in Sicyon that resulted in his father's assassination and his own clandestine exile to Argos at age seven.

Returning to Sicyon in 251 BC at the head of an expedition of exiles, Aratus successfully liberated the city from tyranny by exploiting a clandestine entry route over the defensive walls. He subsequently integrated Sicyon into the Achaean League, representing the League's first admission of a Dorian polis.

Elected strategos seventeen times beginning in 245 BC, Aratus systematically expanded the influence of the Achaean League through strategic acquisitions, most notably capturing the heavily fortified and previously impregnable citadel of Acrocorinth from Macedonian control.

Faced with the expansionist pressures of Spartan King Cleomenes III, Aratus orchestrated a strategic pivot by securing an alliance with Antigonus III Doson of Macedon. This coalition neutralized the Spartan threat through a decisive victory at the Battle of Sellasia.

In his later years, Aratus participated in the Social War as a principal advisor to Philip V of Macedon. His remarkable political longevity concluded with his death in 213 BC, which historical tradition attributes to poisoning ordered by the Macedonian king.
